objective: Assess acute arterial occlusion and deep vein thrombosis in a limb

brief.situation: 14:20 in the emergency department. You are the nurse in a monitored room. Mrs. Lindqvist, 68, has had sudden pain in her right calf and foot since 12:30. She has atrial fibrillation and stopped her anticoagulant a week ago 'because of the bruises'.
handover: Triage: ESI 2. Heart rate 104 irregular, blood pressure 148/86, SpO2 96%. The right foot is pale and cool.
The physician has examined her, suspects an acute arterial occlusion and has ordered IV heparin now, nothing by mouth, and the leg kept dependent.
Unit protocol: any new numbness or weakness in the limb is a threatened limb; the physician and vascular surgery are called at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and treat as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Ischemia advances without anticoagulation. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

Heparin slows clot propagation but does not open the artery, so the limb still becomes threatened. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point where sensation and then movement fail: a threatened limb. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of irreversible muscle and nerve injury. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
Vascular surgery called within 5 minutes of new sensory or motor loss (unit protocol).
The ordered heparin started within 5 minutes of reaching the room (unit practice).
A focused assessment or question: about 1 min.
About 10 minutes for vascular surgery to arrive and take her for revascularization; a discharge or a clinic plan about 10 minutes.

A heat pack on an insensate ischemic foot burns it within minutes, and elevation lowers perfusion pressure. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

why.question: Mrs. Lindqvist's foot has gone numb and weak. What does that mean, and what do you do?

parts.label: What it means
parts.criteria: Sudden pain, pallor, coolness and absent pulses with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation are an embolic arterial occlusion, not a DVT; new numbness and weakness mean the limb is threatened and time to irreversible injury is short.
parts.modelAnswer: This is an embolic arterial occlusion from her atrial fibrillation, not a clot in a vein. Now she has lost sensation and movement, so the limb is threatened and the muscle can die within hours.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Physician and vascular surgery now; heparin running; leg dependent, no heat, no elevation; nothing by mouth; hand off the times.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the physician and vascular surgery now, keep the heparin running, the leg down and protected with no heat, nothing to eat, and hand off the onset and when the numbness began.

noProgress.rationale: An ischemic, threatened limb still in a department room an hour on is harm here.

unsafe.headline: Heat and elevation on an ischemic leg
unsafe.body: An ischemic limb stays dependent. It can't feel heat, so a warm pack burns it, and elevation lowers the pressure pushing blood in.

worsened.headline: Irreversible ischemia
worsened.body: Necrosis can begin within about six hours. New sensory or motor loss is the signal to get vascular surgery at once.

wrongRoute.headline: Sent home
wrongRoute.body: An acute arterial occlusion is an emergency for vascular surgery, not a clinic appointment.

target.headline: Limb rescued in time
target.body: Heparin at once, Doppler pulses, the leg dependent, and the neuro change called within minutes. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: To theater, with delays
recovered.body: Check how long heparin took and how long the numbness went before the call.

time_up.headline: Still waiting
time_up.body: A threatened limb is measured in hours.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sudden pain with a pale, cold foot and no pulses in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation is an embolic arterial occlusion. A DVT swells and is warm; this foot is white and cold. Heparin goes in at once and the leg stays dependent, protected and unheated. New numbness and weakness mean a threatened limb: the physician and vascular surgery are called within minutes.

posQ.ask: While the team takes over: how should the ischemic leg be positioned?
posQ.explain: The extremity should be placed in a dependent position to maximize perfusion.

sixQ.ask: While you assess: which of these points to an arterial occlusion rather than a DVT?
sixQ.explain: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia and paralysis are the classic picture of acute arterial occlusion.
